parts.label: Understand
parts.title: Choose the denominator that matters
parts.body:
A model invoice is one component of an AI service. Choose a unit that corresponds to a finished business outcome, such as a correctly resolved case, a decision delivered within policy, or an accepted draft. Cost per prompt makes a cheap failed answer look efficient. Define the quality bar and count every eligible request that reaches the workflow, including failures, repeats, and cases handed back to people.

For one period, calculate total incremental cost: model calls and retries, retrieval and storage, platform and integration, evaluation, security, monitoring, support, human review, corrections, and adoption work. Distinguish one-time build expense from continuing cost and record the allocation method for shared infrastructure. The FinOps allocation framework is useful for deciding how shared technology costs attach to products or teams. Finance should decide whether the comparison uses incremental cost, fully loaded cost, or both; label the result.

Compare the old and new paths at equivalent quality. If the new system resolves cheaper routine cases while hard cases remain with people, the human team's average cost may rise even when total cost falls. The denominator, volume mix, and quality standard belong beside every headline figure.

example.title: The denominator changes the answer
example.body: Illustrative month: 10,000 eligible requests incur $24,000 in model, retrieval, and platform charges, plus $16,000 in review and support. Only 8,000 meet the agreed quality bar. Cost per request is $4; cost per successful completion is $5 before one-time build expense. If the old workflow costs $4.70 per correct completion, this version has yet to earn a cost claim.

exercise.title: Define a cost unit
exercise.body: Pick a workflow and write the numerator, denominator, quality criterion, reporting period, and owner of each cost component. State what happens to the unit cost when human review time doubles.

sources: FinOps Framework: allocation of shared technology costs
NIST AI RMF Core: evaluation and production monitoring

parts.label: Practice
parts.title: Model volume, quality, and review together
parts.body:
A unit-cost model should expose its drivers. Use eligible volume × adoption × successful completion to estimate completed AI-assisted units. Then estimate human time for every assisted case, including exceptions and correction, and the cost of the traditional path for cases that remain outside the tool. Include fixed platform and team costs. These assumptions are related: if wider adoption reaches harder cases, success and review time may change.

Run at least three scenarios: expected, weaker adoption with more review, and high volume with provider price or latency changes. Show total workflow cost and cost per correct outcome in each. A low cost per model output is irrelevant when the workflow requires expensive verification. Record a break-even condition in operational terms: for example, the minimum share of eligible cases completed correctly with no more than a specified review time.

Check capacity constraints as well as arithmetic. If each case needs eight minutes of human review, a plan for 50,000 monthly cases consumes roughly 6,667 review hours. The number is illustrative and follows 50,000 × 8 ÷ 60. Ask who will provide those hours before claiming the target volume.

example.title: Three complete workflow scenarios
example.body: Assume 50,000 eligible cases per month. The old path costs $8 per case and correctly completes 95%: $400,000 ÷ 47,500 correct cases = $8.42 each. In the base case, 70% adopt AI (35,000 attempts); 80% succeed (28,000). The 7,000 failures and 15,000 non-adopted cases go through the old path, which correctly completes 20,900 of those 22,000. AI variable cost is $1.20 for model calls including retries, $2 for human review, and $0.40 for corrections per attempt: $126,000. Add $30,000 shared fixed cost and $176,000 for the old path. Total $332,000 ÷ 48,900 correct cases = $6.79. The narrower $156,000 ÷ 28,000 = $5.57 per AI-assisted success omits fallback and is not the enterprise comparison. In the downside case, 40% adopt and 70% succeed: 14,000 AI successes; 36,000 old-path cases yield 34,200 correct. Retries/model, doubled review, and corrections total $6.60 per 20,000 AI attempts ($132,000); add $30,000 fixed and $288,000 old path. $450,000 ÷ 48,200 = $9.34. At scale, assume 100,000 eligible cases, 75% adoption, 85% AI success, $3.55 variable cost per AI attempt, and $40,000 fixed cost. The 75,000 attempts yield 63,750 AI successes; 36,250 old-path cases yield 34,438 correct (rounded). Total $596,250 ÷ about 98,188 correct = $6.07, against an old-path baseline of $8.42. These figures are invented, and the old path is assumed to process all AI failures at its original $8 cost and 95% success. Under base adoption and costs, solving [30,000 + 35,000 × 3.60 + (50,000 − 35,000s) × 8] ÷ [35,000s + (50,000 − 35,000s) × 0.95] < $8.42 gives an AI success rate s above roughly 53%. Recalculate if fallback capacity, cost, or quality changes.

exercise.title: Build the scenario table
exercise.body: Create rows for eligible volume, adoption, success, retries, review minutes, fixed cost, variable cost, and cost per correct completion. Enter your own documented assumptions for three scenarios. Identify the two assumptions that most change the investment choice.

sources: NIST AI RMF Playbook: measuring operational performance

parts.label: Operate
parts.title: Assign cost and quality ownership
parts.body:
A model gateway can expose usage by product, but someone still has to reconcile vendor charges, shared platform expense, and the business outcome. Assign a product owner for successful completions, an engineering owner for usage and latency, a finance owner for allocation, and a control owner for evaluation and review. Agree a monthly variance threshold that triggers examination; set its value from the organization's budget and appetite, not a universal AI benchmark.

Watch cost per correct completion as the model, prompts, retrieval corpus, or provider changes. A switch that lowers token price may increase retries or human corrections. A more capable model may cost more per call but reduce the total workflow expense. Test changes on representative cases and measure the full path before switching at scale. Keep a dated cost model with the assumptions and version used for every investment decision.

For multinational operations, avoid silently pooling dissimilar costs or service results. Labour rates, language evaluation, data handling requirements, and vendor contracts may differ between Canada and EU countries. Report common units and the local inputs behind them so the executive can see whether an apparent regional difference is performance or accounting.

example.title: A cheaper model that costs more
example.body: A proposed model cuts inference cost by $0.30 per case on 100,000 cases but adds one minute of review at an illustrative $30 per hour. The extra review costs $50,000 versus $30,000 saved on inference. Test whether quality gains elsewhere offset the difference before switching.

exercise.title: Set an operating review
exercise.body: Draft a one-page monthly cost report with usage, success rate, cost per correct outcome, review time, variance from forecast, and changes in case mix. Name who investigates a variance and who can approve a model substitution.

sources: NIST AI RMF Core: change management and monitoring

parts.label: Apply
parts.title: Defend the economics to the CFO
parts.body:
An investment packet should show a traceable bridge from eligible volume to adoption, correct outcomes, total cost, and benefit. Put assumptions beside the number they produce. Disclose the comparison quality standard and whether costs are incremental or fully loaded. List one-time implementation spending separately, then show a payback calculation only if the benefits will actually be recognized in cash or an agreed operational value measure.

The CFO may ask what happens if adoption is late, model prices rise, or a new review requirement is added. Answer with scenario results and a spending limit. If the case depends on perfect adoption or zero review, the next decision is likely a bounded test. A useful recommendation also names an exit path, including the cost of returning to the old workflow or moving providers.

Choose a threshold for continued funding that the business can measure. For example: maintain the quality bar, attain a specified cost per correct case for two reporting periods, and show no increase in escalations. These are policy choices to approve, not facts inferred from a model benchmark.

example.title: A concise investment request
example.body: Illustrative request: $120,000 for a three-month controlled pilot of 10,000 cases, including integration and review. Expand only if cost per correct case falls below the documented old path and the reopen rate stays within its agreed limit in two consecutive periods. Finance validates the cost bridge; the service executive owns the result.

exercise.title: Answer a skeptical CFO
exercise.body: Write a memo with base, downside, and scale scenarios; one-time and recurring costs; cost per correct outcome; a quality countermeasure; and the break-even condition. Have a peer alter one assumption and recalculate the recommendation.

sources: NIST AI RMF Core: manage and monitor
